bothSidesReview.eligibility: On-record opposition from three NAMED organizations, each in its own published analysis of this bill or its immediate predecessor: the Electronic Frontier Foundation (a May 15, 2025 analysis of S. 1748 itself), the American Civil Liberties Union (named policy counsel, on the House and Senate versions), and Fight for the Future (a statement issued the day the Senate Commerce Committee acted, August 5, 2026). Support is equally on the record: the sponsor, both party leaders as original cosponsors, and a joint sponsor statement of June 29, 2026. This satisfies the docs/BOTH-SIDES.md trigger 'a formal opposition letter or statement from a named organization' without any recorded vote on S. 1748 at all -- the section says so explicitly rather than implying a contested vote. Not false balance: no opposition was sought out to fill a slot, and every position that could not be sourced was removed (see resolution).
bothSidesReview.verbSymmetry: pass -- only argues/argued/says/said/contends-class neutral verbs appear across both sides; none of notes/points out/claims/alleges/acknowledges/admits/concedes. Verified mechanically against scripts/tracker-gate.js's own ASYMMETRIC_VERBS regex over the extracted section: 0 hits. The EFF's own section heading containing the word 'claims' was deliberately NOT quoted, and two EFF sentences whose source wording nests a quoted term ('reasonable care', 'compulsive usage') were rendered as attributed paraphrase rather than as a quote that could not match verbatim.
bothSidesReview.stripTest: pass -- every argumentative sentence in the section names its holder (Blackburn/Blumenthal, the APA, the EFF, Jenna Leventoff of the ACLU, Sarah Philips of Fight for the Future) and resolves to a stored source. Structural facts stated in the article's own voice are bill-text or Congress.gov record facts only (harm counts, section numbers, action history, vote tallies), never contested characterizations. Seven unsourceable named positions were REMOVED rather than softened -- see the omission rows.
bothSidesReview.vehicleBill:
HUMAN-verified 2026-08-28 (Opus, in-conversation), across every vehicle the stored record discloses, asserting nothing from memory. (1) S. 1748 itself: Congress.gov relatedbills returns ZERO related bills, so the record identifies no companion and no vehicle for the Senate text. Laws: null. (2) H.R. 7757, the KIDS Act, is the only measure in this policy area to have received a floor vote in the 119th Congress (267-117, Roll 228, 2026-06-29, under suspension of the rules; received in the Senate 2026-07-13). Its OWN relatedbills record lists two bills, H.R. 6289 and H.R. 6437 -- S. 1748 is NOT among them, so Congress.gov links the two KOSA-adjacent measures to each other nowhere in its data. The article therefore describes H.R. 7757 as a different measure, never as KOSA's companion or vehicle. (3) THE RECORD SURPRISE, and the reason the vehicle check is human-only: the KIDS Act does not merely omit the duty of care, it EXPRESSLY DISCLAIMS it -- section 213(c)(2) provides that nothing in its harms provision may be construed to 'impose a duty of care on a provider of a covered platform.' The pre-retrofit article said only that the House bill 'does not include' the standard, which understated a disclaimer the bill text spells out. Verified by reading the stored engrossed text, not from the CRS summary (which does not mention it). (4) HISTORICAL vehicle, re-verified rather than restated: docs/BOTH-SIDES.md records that KOSA's 91-3 Senate vote rode S. 2073. The stored record confirms the tally and goes further than the doc -- S. 2073 was introduced as the Eliminate Useless Reports Act of 2023, a title 31 agency-reporting bill, which is what makes 'unrelated vehicle' a sourced fact rather than a characterization; the Senate's action was to concur in the House amendment WITH a further amendment (SA 3021), not to pass KOSA as such. S. 2073 Laws: null, last action 'Message on Senate action sent to the House.' 2024-07-31. The patch-console panel checkbox is James's to tick; this ledger line is the durable record of the check itself.

DELTA RE-CHECK 2026-08-31 (Opus, in-conversation, live Congress.gov API). Neither tracked bill has moved since the 2026-08-27 retrofit: S. 1748 latest action is still 2026-08-05, Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably, with 3 actions and an empty laws array; H.R. 7757 latest action is still 2026-07-13, Received in the Senate and referred to Commerce. The substitute text is still unpublished. So this delta changes no status claim -- it adds only the position the retrofit had to omit for want of a fetchable source. Checked because the B1 lesson is that a refresh must re-verify the bill AND its companions live, and because the last KOSA refresh was triggered by exactly such a move.
bothSidesReview.staleness: The staleness trigger for this retrofit was npm run stale flagging 119-S-1748 as having moved to 2026-08-05, newer than the article's frozen 2026-07-17 date. That movement is now the article's lead fact. Every referenced bill was re-checked against the date this refresh stamps, not the date it replaces: S. 1748 (2026-08-05), H.R. 7757 (2026-07-13), S. 1409 and S. 2073 (118th Congress, both final). tracker-gate is handed --as-of by publish-article.

supporterLens.note: Round 1: YES with two non-blocking findings, both adopted -- the sponsors' quotation had been cut short of its closing clause, and the APA paragraph drew on only one of that source's five stated goals after four coalition organizations and an executive quotation had been stripped from it for accuracy. ONE PROPOSED SPAN WAS WRONG AND WAS CORRECTED: the reviewer proposed quoting through 'allow Big Tech's predatory business model to remain intact', but the stored page encodes that apostrophe as the HTML entity ’, so no quotation spanning it can resolve byte-for-byte; the quotation was split around it instead. Round 2: NO -- BLOCKING, and the mirror image of the opponent lens's own blocking finding. The opponents' section makes the age-verification argument twice (the EFF's 'effectively mandating age verification' and the ACLU's 'verify the ages of their users'), while S. 1748 section 112(c)(2) expressly disclaims requiring exactly that and appeared nowhere in the article -- not in the both-sides section and not in What the Bill Would Require. The reviewer grepped all four stored opponent files for '112' and 'age gat' and found no rebuttal of the disclaimer before proposing it, so the point goes to the supporters unanswered on the record as stored. Adopted verbatim. Round 3: YES, no further findings. Declined the opportunity to also quote section 112(c)(1) (the personal-data-collection disclaimer), reasoning that it is a related but distinct point about data collection rather than about verification mandates and would not sharpen this rebuttal -- a restraint worth recording, since the easy move was to take it. Endorsed the paragraph split that moved the bill's-own-text rebuttal out from under the 281-word organizational-support paragraph, and re-confirmed the 4-to-5 paragraph ratio as fair given that the opponents draw on roughly four times the raw source material across their four stored documents.
supporterLens.proportionCheck: Independently measured across rounds 2 and 3: supporters ~480 words to opponents ~500, against stored source corpora of roughly 2,040 supporter words to 7,980 opponent words. Both reviewers concluded the paragraph ratio is, if anything, more generous to supporters than the underlying record would justify.
supporterLens.delta20260831: REFUSED at delta round 1, SIGNED OFF at delta round 2. Its blocking item: the first version of the CDT paragraph quoted only the objections and omitted that the letter commends the committee focus on protecting children online and affirmatively backs a named competing bill, which made CDT read as more totalizingly anti-regulation than its own source shows. Accepted in full. At round 2 it read the letter again, confirmed the fix against the source rather than against the description of the fix, and specifically judged whether the fix had OVERCORRECTED -- concluding it had not, because the praise gets a clause rather than a sentence and the KOSA-specific objections are unhedged. It also independently re-found the missing closing paragraph tag. Non-blocking note recorded: the opponent side now runs about 48 percent longer than the supporter side, which it attributes to the record (four named opponent organisations against one supporter organisation whose statement the article itself date-bounds to a predecessor bill) rather than to padding.

opponentLens.note: Round 1: NO -- THREE BLOCKING findings, all substantive and all accepted. (a) Coalition breadth: after the four unsourceable LGBTQ organizations were removed, the article paraphrased Fight for the Future's self-description instead of quoting it, discarding the one sourced statement of who the opposing coalition actually is; now quoted verbatim, cut at '(KOSA)' on the reviewer's own reasoning that the source's next clause concerns the separate SCREEN Act. (b) THE STRONGEST FINDING OF THE SESSION: the supporters' section quotes the bill's section 102(b)(1) and 102(b)(2) carve-outs as the answer to the censorship objection, and the opponents' section never responded to them -- while the stored EFF May 2025 analysis carries a section headed 'Carveouts Don't Fix the First Amendment Problem' doing exactly that. An unanswered rebuttal where a sourced answer sits unused in a stored file is a fairness defect, not a mere omission. Added as its own paragraph. (c) The February 2024 revisions were narrated in neutral own-voice using the EFF as the factual source while dropping the EFF's own assessment of them, which reads as though the revisions satisfied the objection; that assessment is now quoted. TWO NON-BLOCKING findings: one adopted (a stronger verbatim quote for the compulsive-usage point), one PARTLY REJECTED -- the proposed 'reasonable care' replacement span ends 'the government-in this case the FTC-claims is harmful', and 'claims' is on the banned verb-symmetry list, which the scripted gate greps across the whole section without exempting text inside quotation marks; the paraphrase stands and the reviewer was told why. A fifth, additive finding (disparate impact on small platforms) was adopted. ONE PROPOSED SPAN WAS WRONG AND WAS CORRECTED: the reviewer proposed quoting 'those improvements do not cure KOSA's core First Amendment problems' and advised normalizing the curly apostrophe to straight 'per site convention' -- that would have broken the receipt, since matching is byte-level against the stored file; the quotation was split around the apostrophe instead. Round 2: YES. Re-verified every quoted span byte-for-byte against its own holder's file including the split-quote workaround, re-ran the verb-symmetry grep including text inside quotation marks (zero hits), confirmed supporters-first, and independently measured proportion at 480/500 words. Round 3 was requested by the coordinator rather than by the reviewer, because a supporter-side rebuttal (section 112(c)) was added AFTER the round-2 sign-off and it would not have been honest to ship a sign-off given against different text.
opponentLens.round3: Round 3: YES. Independently grepped all four stored opponent files for '112', 'age gat', 'age verif', 'disclaim', 'carve', 'rule of construction' and 'construed', and confirmed the supporter reviewer's finding that none of them engages section 112(c) or the disclaimer-vs-practical-effect argument -- most hits were navigation boilerplate or teaser blurbs for unrelated posts. Reasoning for signing off rather than blocking: unlike its own round-1 finding (b), where the viewpoint-carveout rebuttal was absent from the article entirely, the age-verification objection already has a substantive rebuttal sitting in reading order immediately after the new section 112(c) sentence -- the EFF's 'effectively mandating age verification' and the ACLU's 'verify the ages of their users' both make the formal-limit-does-not-stop-practical-effect point in substance, so the supporters' claim is not structurally left unanswered. It also advised AGAINST the coordinator's offered alternative of rewording or reordering to make the adjacency explicit, on the ground that forcing a cross-reference would read as own-voice editorializing rather than sourced attribution.
opponentLens.delta20260831: SIGNED OFF at delta round 1 and again at delta round 2 after the paragraph changed substantially. Round 2 was asked directly whether the supporter-driven fix had defanged CDT, and answered no: all three KOSA-specific arguments survive verbatim, the S. 4199 material is confined to an explicitly labelled fourth measure, and the passage ends on CDT own criticism rather than on its concession. It also corrected a premise in its own brief -- Fight for the Future statement is dated 2026-08-05, one day AFTER the CDT letter, so FFTF and not CDT is the most current document on the page, which makes the existing chronological ordering correct.

bothSidesReview.thirdHeading: 'How the bill has changed in response' is retained from the pre-retrofit article and is permitted by docs/BOTH-SIDES.md as a neutral heading for on-record context. Its content changed substantially: the unsourceable claim that four named LGBTQ organizations dropped their opposition after the February 2024 revision was REMOVED, and the heading now carries only (a) the EFF's own account of what that revision changed, (b) where those two changes land in the S. 1748 text, and (c) the fact that the August 5, 2026 substitute is unpublished, so no side's argument about the current Senate text can be reported at all.
bothSidesReview.crossModelVerify: Hostile source-only Sonnet pass, 2026-08-27, one round. VERDICT: DEFECTS FOUND, FABRICATIONS 0. The verifier extracted all 34 double-quoted spans from the article body programmatically and checked each against the file its surrounding sentence attributes it to, then machine-checked all 98 non-empty sourceSpan values in the then-107-row ledger against the textFile named by each row's own sourceFile via the ledger's sources[] map -- 0 mismatches. It separately grep-confirmed that the removed items (the Evans quotation, the ACLU 'censor protected speech' quotation, the misattributed 'design features' phrase, the four named coalition organizations, and the stale 'has not received a committee vote' line) are genuinely absent from the current article. It independently re-derived the cosponsor party split by parsing all 76 rows (42 R / 33 D / 1 I) and verified all five section-number citations character-for-character, including the 'or' vs 'and' connectors. Categories returned clean: misattribution none, polarity/direction none, timeline/scope none, section-numbers none. THREE findings, all resolved: (1) UNSOURCED, real -- the clause describing the 2024 package as one 'which incorporated KOSA together with an update to children's online privacy law' was a content characterization in the article's own voice that no stored file supports; inherited from the pre-retrofit article and carrying no covering ledger row. Replaced with a fact that IS in the record (body.history.p2.i). (2) MINOR but real, a quotation-boundary defect -- see finding.sponsor-quote-boundary; removed. (3) MINOR, flagged per the letter of the audit instructions rather than as a defect -- the general 60-vote cloture assertion had no corpus source. Rather than adjudicate it as common knowledge, both places making that point are now bound to the roll-call sheet's own 'Required For Majority' line (body.history.p2.j). The verifier also correctly observed that the lens sign-offs and this field read PENDING at the time it ran; they were in flight and are recorded here.
bothSidesReview.residualDeclined: RECORDED, DECLINED, NOT CHURNED (2026-08-27). In round 3 the opponent reviewer surfaced genuinely unused ACLU material that states the formal-versus-practical argument explicitly -- 'The Paxton decision limits the legality of age verification laws strictly to sexual content', 'But in practice, laws like KOSA would incentivize age verification for a wide variety of content', and 'That could result in, for example, adults undergoing invasive age checks just to watch YouTube videos' -- all three verified verbatim in data/ref-text/org-aclu-kosa.txt, all three in the ACLU's own voice rather than nested quotation, and each deliberately cut short of the source's nested 'harmful' quotation marks. It was NOT added, and the reviewer that found it explicitly called its absence non-blocking. Reasons: both lenses had already signed off on the text as it stands; the reviewer's own analysis is that the point is already carried by two quotations sitting in reading order right after the sentence it would answer; and adding further opponent material after a supporter-side addition would reopen the balance question for the other lens. Trading one lens's non-blocking preference for the other's is churn, not convergence. Logged here so the material is auditable and easy to pick up in a later refresh rather than invisible -- it is the strongest single candidate for the next cycle on this article.
bothSidesReview.convergence: DELTA 2026-08-31 (CDT). The one position this retrofit had to omit for lack of a fetchable source is now on the page. cdt.org 403s every scripted path; a real-browser session cleared it on 2026-08-27 and the August 4, 2026 letter to Senate Commerce -- sent the day before the committee acted, and the most on-point current-Congress opposition document that exists -- was stored verbatim with its insights companion. Seven claims added, all receipted. The delta was re-verified by a hostile SONNET source pass and re-reviewed by both lenses, which also makes this ledger cross-model for the first time: the retrofit recorded opus as both drafter and auditor.

resolution:
Phase 5 retrofit of a pre-lane both-sides tracker, published 2026-07-17 with sources LINKED but NOT STORED and no claim ledger -- the standing liability class. Trigger: npm run stale flagged 119-S-1748 as having moved on 2026-08-05, newer than the frozen article date.

SOURCING. 26 sources fetched and STORED: 2 bill texts (S. 1748 introduced, H.R. 7757 engrossed), 17 Congress.gov and Senate.gov records (status, full action histories, cosponsors, text versions, related bills, CRS summaries for four bills across two Congresses; both Senate roll-call sheets; the Senate leadership roster), and 5 organization or member statements. Before the retrofit the article carried 10 bare links and nothing on disk.

STATUS REFRESH, the staleness fix. S. 1748 is no longer merely referred to committee: on 2026-08-05 the Commerce Committee ordered it reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably. THAT SUBSTITUTE TEXT IS NOT PUBLISHED -- Congress.gov lists exactly one text version, the text introduced 2025-05-14 -- so the article states the absence rather than describing text nobody can read, the same framing the S. 1748 bill page already uses. The article also now records that being ordered reported is the first of the three steps the predecessor bill logged (ordered reported, then reported, then placed on the calendar), and that Congress.gov records neither later step for S. 1748.

SEVEN POSITIONS OMITTED, none softened. (1) A quotation attributed to a named living individual, APA chief executive Arthur C. Evans Jr., that does not exist in the APA source the article itself cited -- the single most serious defect found, and the defamation class this lane exists for. (2) An ACLU quotation, censor protected speech for fear of being held legally liable, absent from the ACLU source. (3) The quoted term design features attributed to the ACLU when it belongs to the EFF -- right quotation, wrong holder, and a defect a gate checking only whether a quote exists SOMEWHERE would pass. (4) Three subject-matter examples attributed to the ACLU that its source does not contain. (5) Four organizations named as coalition members by a source that names none. (6) The Center for Democracy and Technology, whose position could not be sourced because cdt.org returns HTTP 403 to the fetcher on every path tried, including an August 4 2026 coalition letter to the Senate Commerce Committee sent the day before the committee acted. (7) A claim that four named LGBTQ organizations dropped their opposition after the February 2024 revision, unsourced for all four. Two further unsourced items were removed: an unnamed-holder Supporters say attribution, and a bundled four-organization attribution.

ONE POSITION RESCUED RATHER THAN OMITTED. Fight for the Future was named as an opponent with no source. A statement it issued on 2026-08-05, the day the committee acted, was fetched and stored, so the position now rests on the organization's own words and its named campaign director.

THE RECORD SURPRISE, which is where the handoff said to expect one. The House KIDS Act does not merely omit KOSA's duty of care: section 213(c)(2) expressly provides that nothing in its harms provision may be construed to impose a duty of care on a provider of a covered platform. The CRS summary does not mention the disclaimer; only the bill text carries it. The pre-retrofit article said only that the House bill does not include the standard. Separately, Congress.gov identifies NO related bills for S. 1748, and H.R. 7757's own related-bill record names two other bills but not S. 1748 -- so the two measures are linked nowhere in the data, and the article describes H.R. 7757 as a different measure rather than as a companion.

CONVERGENCE. One hostile source-only cross-model pass (0 fabrications; 3 findings, all resolved) plus three rounds of each adversarial lens. Both lenses independently found THE SAME DEFECT CLASS IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS: an argument pressed on one side with a sourced answer sitting unused in a stored file on the other. The opponent lens caught that the supporters' section 102(b) carve-outs went unanswered while the EFF's Carveouts Don't Fix the First Amendment Problem section sat unused; the supporter lens caught that the opponents' age-verification argument, made twice, went unanswered while section 112(c)(2)'s express disclaimer sat unused. Both are now in the article. Three reviewer-proposed spans were WRONG and were corrected rather than pasted: two could not resolve because the stored sources encode apostrophes as an HTML entity and as a curly character, and one would have imported the banned verb claims inside a quotation, which the scripted gate does not exempt.
notes:
Phase 5 wave-1 retrofit, second of the three remaining July trackers. Joins qa-regression.

FOR THE NEXT CYCLE ON THIS ARTICLE, in priority order:
1. Retry the Center for Democracy and Technology. Its August 4 2026 coalition letter to Senate Commerce is the most on-point current-Congress opposition document that exists, and it is unreachable only because of bot protection, not because it does not exist. A different fetch path would let a real position back into the article.
2. The declined ACLU Paxton material recorded in bothSidesReview.residualDeclined is the strongest single candidate for addition, already verified verbatim.
3. The substitute text ordered reported on 2026-08-05 will eventually be published. When it is, this article needs a full re-read, not a delta: the analysis and both sides currently describe the introduced text, which is the only version that exists on Congress.gov today.

FOR FABLE'S QC TO POKE AT:
- The read-time line still says ~7 min while the body grew from 1,333 to 2,403 words. It was left alone deliberately: the site has no computed convention (existing articles range from 83 to 487 words per stated minute, and the 119th-congress-tracker shows 6 min for 2,924 words), so bumping this one article would make it inconsistent with its siblings in the other direction. This is a site-wide question, not a KOSA question, and it is James's or Fable's call, not a unilateral fix.
- data/ref-text/record-congress-hr-7757-summary.txt is stored as fetch provenance but is deliberately NOT registered on the ledger. Registering an unused source would widen the pool that tracker-gate's quotes-stored check searches, which loosens the gate for no benefit.
- The stored sources are stamped 2026-08-28 while the publish stamps 2026-08-27. This is not an error and not something this session introduced: fetch-reference.js stamps UTC while publish-article.js stamps local date by deliberate design, and the two differ for a few hours each night. Worth knowing before it looks like a future date.
- The APA source is the weakest link in the supporter set. It is a 2023 Washington Update about the 118th Congress bill, and it is the ONLY organizational support document on disk. The article date-bounds it explicitly and the supporter lens endorsed that framing as honest rather than diminishing, but a current-Congress supporter organization statement would materially strengthen this side and none was found.
- The eligibility rationale rests on named-organization statements, NOT on a recorded vote, because no recorded vote on S. 1748 exists. The article says so in its first both-sides sentence. Confirm that reads as a structural trigger under docs/BOTH-SIDES.md rather than as an invitation to false balance.

VEHICLE-BILL SIGN-OFF: James approved 2026-08-28 (verbal-remote, recorded per the SAVE precedent — the panel checkbox is per-publish and this refresh published via CLI, so the ledger is the durable record). Scope of the approval, explained to and confirmed by James: the article tracks S. 1748 under its own number and claims no vehicle (Congress.gov relates zero bills in either direction); the committee substitute is unpublished and the article says so rather than describing it; H.R. 7757 is presented as a rival approach, not a KOSA vehicle, per its own Sec. 213(c)(2) duty-of-care disclaimer. A future record change showing KOSA text riding another bill is a refresh trigger, not an error in this version.
